ideas.working_title: Do Language Models Read the Log or the Labels? A Label-Intervention Protocol for Semantics-Aware Next-Activity Prediction at Varying Training Sizes
ideas.problem_rq: Three results received pull in different directions. Weytjens and Weber (BPM 2026 Forum chapter; arXiv HTML read in full) show on seven 4TU logs (BPI12, BPI15, BPI17, BPI19, three BPI20 sub-logs) that a counting argmax baseline matches or approaches GPT-2 and Qwen-3 models up to 4B, but their 'direct sequence modeling' with vocabulary adaptation discards activity-label text and they separate it from text-serialisation approaches. Padella, de Leoni and Dumas (arXiv 2601.11468, read in full) show Gemini 2.5 Flash beating CatBoost and PGTNet with only 100 traces and, via semantic hashing of labels, that part of the gain comes from label semantics (BPI12 total-time MAE 6508 unhashed vs 9246 hashed at 100 traces), but with one proprietary model, two tasks that are not next-activity prediction, one public log, and no trivial baseline. Kourani, Antonov, Berti and van der Aalst show knowledge-driven hallucination (reverting to standard flows against reversed or shuffled inputs) only for text-to-model generation. RQ1: As a function of training-set size (50 traces to full), how much of a text-serialised predictor's next-activity accuracy is attributable to activity-label semantics rather than log-derived statistics, measured against argmax, Markov and one-hot LSTM baselines that are label-invariant by construction? RQ2: When labels are rewritten so that their natural-language meaning implies a flow that conflicts with the log, do semantics-aware predictors (sentence-embedding classifiers, 1.5-4B instruction-tuned LLMs, LoRA-tuned small models) follow the labels or the evidence, and does this evidence fidelity depend on training size?
ideas.why_matters: Predictive process monitoring is being re-tooled around LLMs on the strength of data-scarce wins, yet the systematic negative result (argmax parity) tested a design that cannot use semantics, and the positive result used a proprietary model that cannot be rerun. Organisations with small logs are exactly those for whom a semantic prior could help or mislead; a label-intervention protocol gives a reproducible way to measure which, and the fidelity construct connects predictive monitoring to the evidence-fidelity problem documented for process modeling. Whatever the direction of the result, the protocol and the learning-curve tables on public logs address the 'when do LLM semantics help' gap named in the agents-BPM digest (gap 2) and the evidence-fidelity gap (gap 3).
ideas.contribution: Technical and empirical. (1) A measurement protocol: an intervention on activity labels (original, anonymised codes, synonym-preserving paraphrase, meaning-conflicting relabeling, reversed stage names) that identifies semantic dependence and evidence fidelity for any next-activity predictor, with label-agnostic baselines serving as built-in manipulation checks. (2) A reproducible empirical finding: learning curves over training-set size for trivial, classical and semantics-aware predictors on the same public 4TU logs, with trace-clustered intervals. (3) A conflict-set construction method yielding prefixes where the log-majority next activity differs from the label-implied next activity, enabling a fidelity rate. A null result on semantic gain is itself the answer to the open question and reconciles the Weytjens-Weber and Padella findings.

ideas.difference: Weytjens and Weber discard label text (vocabulary adaptation) and do not vary training size; this study keeps label text and varies both. Padella et al. only remove semantics (hashing) with one API model on time and activity-occurrence KPIs; this study adds the adversarial direction (labels that conflict with the log), uses open 1.5-4B models and embedding classifiers that run on CPU, targets next-activity prediction, and reports argmax and Markov baselines in the same tables. Kourani, Antonov et al. test text inputs, not event logs; this study ports their reversed/shuffled logic to log-grounded prediction and quantifies it as a fidelity rate. Rebmann et al. test semantics-aware tasks with fine-tuning but without a label-intervention control or learning curves; Fertig, Kirchdorfer and Sesterhenn (ECML PKDD 2026 workshops, abstract only) compare paradigms but, per the abstract, without label manipulation or training-size curves.
ideas.design: Factorial design: public logs (BPI12, BPI17, BPI20 Prepaid Travel Costs, Travel Permit, Request for Payment, Sepsis Cases, Road Traffic Fines; English-label logs carry the semantic arms because BPI12/17 labels are partly Dutch) x training size (50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2500, full traces; temporal split as in Weytjens and Weber; fixed held-out test prefixes) x label condition (original; anonymised codes; synonym-preserving paraphrase; meaning-conflicting relabeling where label texts are permuted so the implied stage order contradicts the observed flow; reversed stage names) x predictor family. Label-agnostic baselines: counting argmax, first- and second-order Markov with add-k smoothing, small one-hot LSTM. Semantics-aware predictors: kNN and logistic classifiers over sentence-embedding prefix encodings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge-small-en-v1.5), few-shot text-serialised prompting of Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct, Qwen3-1.7B/4B, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini (GGUF 4-bit via llama.cpp on CPU), and LoRA fine-tuning of the 1.5B model at n <= 500 where CPU time allows. Measures: accuracy and macro-F1 (matching Weytjens and Weber), semantic dependence = acc(original) - acc(anonymised), evidence fidelity = share of conflict-set prefixes on which the prediction equals the log-majority rather than the label-implied activity, calibration (ECE) where probabilities exist. Unit of analysis: test prefix nested in trace, log, condition and seed; trace-clustered bootstrap intervals (Miller) and Bayesian intervals where test sets are small (Bowyer et al.). Confirmatory, preregistered: H1 label-agnostic baselines are invariant across label conditions (manipulation check, tolerance 0.5 points); H2 semantic dependence of semantics-aware predictors declines with training size and is not distinguishable from zero at n >= 1000 on the majority of logs; H3 under meaning-conflicting labels the fidelity of semantics-aware predictors at n <= 100 is lower than argmax by a preregistered margin, and the gap closes with n. Exploratory: per-activity error analysis, prompt and serialisation sensitivity, whether semantic gain concentrates in rare activities, CPU-seconds-per-prediction versus accuracy frontier. Test subsampling (500 prefixes per log and condition for LLM arms) fixed in advance; embedding and classical arms use full test sets.

The 'Bac' log used by Padella et al. lives in the IBM processmining GitHub repository and would need to be added to the session; their hospital log is private and not usable.
ideas.risks: Validity: label manipulations can be dismissed as artificial, so the synonym-preserving condition must show that benign rewording does not move results; Dutch labels in BPI12/17 weaken the semantic arm, hence English logs carry H2/H3; the conflict set is a selected subset, so fidelity must be reported with its base rate; small models may be near chance in all conditions, making the LLM arm uninformative (the embedding classifiers and LoRA arm guard against this); many logs x conditions require preregistered primary contrasts. Execution: CPU few-shot inference with long prefixes is prefill-dominated (tens of seconds per prompt for 3-4B models), so LLM arms must be subsampled and intervals will be wide; LoRA on CPU is feasible only for the 1.5B model at small n; temporal splits and prefix construction must match Weytjens and Weber to be comparable.
ideas.journal_audience: Process Science (Springer) or Information Systems (Elsevier) for the journal version; BPM conference or ICPM for a first version; Decision Support Systems as an alternative with a decision-support framing.
ideas.undermining_evidence: A paper already reporting anonymised-label and conflicting-label controls with trivial baselines across training sizes on public logs would remove the gap; the closest candidates found are Padella et al. (hashing only, one API model), Fertig et al. (arXiv 2607.27797) and van Straten et al. (D-TAIA, arXiv 2608.28236), both read at abstract level only, and the Rebmann et al. benchmark release; their full texts should be read before committing. If small open models score at chance under every label condition, the study collapses into a negative result about small models rather than about semantics; if semantic gain is zero even at n = 50 for embedding classifiers, H3 cannot be tested and the paper reduces to a replication of argmax parity.

ideas.working_title: Small Judges, Family Ties: Chance-Corrected Validity, Calibration-Set Requirements, Quantisation Cost and Same-Family Preference Leakage for CPU-Runnable 1-4B LLM Judges
ideas.problem_rq: 'Reliability without Validity' (arXiv 2606.19544, HTML read in full) evaluates 21 API-served judges from 8B upwards and finds exact match overstates Cohen's kappa by 33.8-41.3 points on MT-Bench, rank shifts of up to 14 positions across benchmarks and a consistency-bias paradox; its 541,000-judgment dataset is promised upon publication. Tiwari (arXiv 2609.13824, abstract) evaluates two local 7-8B judges on 300 responses with Pearson correlation only. Lee et al. (ICML 2026) give a plug-in correction that needs a human-labelled calibration set. Preference Leakage (Li et al.; ICLR 2026 per the arXiv comment; full text read) shows frontier judges (GPT-4o, Gemini) favour related student models; Wataoka et al. attribute self-preference to low perplexity; Panickssery et al. to self-recognition; Thakur et al. (GEM 2025) find only the largest judges align with humans and warn that percent agreement misleads. No record received validates quantised 1-4B open judges with chance correction, position swaps, repeated runs and calibration-set curves, or tests whether an off-the-shelf small judge favours outputs of its own model family once candidate quality is held fixed. RQ1: Under a fixed validation protocol on released human- or objectively-labelled sets, do quantised 1-4B open judges reach usable chance-corrected validity on any benchmark subset, and how much does 4-bit versus 8-bit quantisation cost? RQ2: How many human-labelled calibration items (50-400) are needed to bound their error with the Lee et al. correction? RQ3: In a fully crossed generator-family x judge-family design on tasks with objective labels, is there a same-family effect after controlling for the objective quality difference, and is it mediated by the judge's perplexity on the candidate text or moderated by judge size?
ideas.why_matters: Projects without API budgets (student theses, SMEs, public bodies, and this project) will use small local judges, typically from the same family as the generator, to grade RAG answers, process descriptions and decision rationales; enterprise RAG and process-mining benchmarks already report LLM-judge scores as headline metrics without chance-corrected validation (RAG digest gap 1; PM-LLM-Benchmark authors flag judge bias). Whether such judges carry any validity, how much human labelling makes their scores reportable, and whether same-family generate-and-judge designs are confounded are all unanswered in the records received. A clean negative result ('no judge below 4B passes a chance-corrected audit on adversarial pairs') is as useful as a positive one, the calibration-set curves give a concrete labelling budget, and the validation table is a reusable artefact for IS evaluation work.
ideas.contribution: Empirical and methodological. (1) A minimum validation protocol for the no-API regime (Cohen's kappa and Krippendorff's alpha, AB/BA swap consistency, test-retest over runs, verbosity and length conditioning, calibration of stated confidence, Bayesian intervals, Lee-style calibration-set correction) with quantisation as an explicit factor, pre-registered pass criteria and power computed for the Bowyer et al. small-n regime. (2) A validation table for 1-4B judges, absent from the records received, directly comparable to the frontier-judge deflation reported by Norman et al. (3) Calibration-set size curves (50-400 items) quantifying the human labelling needed to report judge-based results with valid intervals. (4) A factorial estimate of the same-family effect with quality fixed by objective labels, separating genuine quality (the 'for a reason' explanation) from familiarity, with perplexity as mechanism check. (5) Released judgments, prompts, perplexities and code for replication on commodity hardware.

ideas.difference: 'Reliability without Validity' covers 8B-100B+ API judges and does not vary quantisation or measure leakage; this study covers the 1-4B CPU regime with quantisation as a factor, adds the calibration-set curves of Lee et al. (which the cohort study lists as future work) and a leakage test. Tiwari uses 7-8B judges, 300 responses from one generator and correlation metrics; this study uses released benchmarks with objective (JudgeBench) and adversarial (LLMBar) labels, chance-corrected agreement and swap audits. Preference Leakage measures leakage toward fine-tuned students using frontier judges and asks about training-data relatedness; here there is no fine-tuning and the question is whether an off-the-shelf small judge favours its own family, the configuration a no-API project actually runs. Wataoka et al. and Panickssery et al. study a judge's preference for its own outputs; here family membership is crossed with judge family in a factorial with quality held fixed by objective labels so the 'legitimately better' explanation is testable. Thakur et al. vary judge size but do not cross generator and judge families and use a clean exam-answer setting. Zheng et al. validate with raw agreement and left self-enhancement 'cannot be determined'; Zhao, Wang and Chen (EMNLP 2026, abstract) use 12-14B models for debiasing, a different question.
ideas.design: Stage 1 (validation, confirmatory). Judges: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, Granite-3.1-2B-Instruct, each at 8-bit and 4-bit GGUF via llama.cpp (quantisation factor), temperature 0 plus three sampled runs on a subsample. Items: MT-bench human judgments ('human' expert votes; the 'gpt4_pair' split supplies published GPT-4 verdicts as a no-API reference judge), LLMBar (419 instances, Natural vs Adversarial), JudgeBench (350 objectively labelled pairs), RewardBench (stratified subsample of 2,985 triplets). Every pair judged in AB and BA order. Baselines: random, always-first, always-longer, lexical-overlap heuristic, published GPT-4 verdicts, published kappa for 8B+ judges from the cohort study as external reference. Measures: exact agreement (for comparability), Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, swap consistency and flip rate, test-retest, verbosity bias conditional on the human label, ECE of stated confidence where available, Bayesian credible intervals (bayes_evals) and trace-level bootstrap; Lee et al. plug-in correction with calibration subsets of 50/100/200/400 items, reporting corrected accuracy intervals versus subset size. Pre-registered pass criterion: kappa >= 0.4 and position consistency >= 0.8. Stage 2 (leakage, confirmatory). Generators: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen3-1.7B, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, Phi-3.5-mini, Granite-3.1-2B produce answers to about 300 prompts with objective labels (JudgeBench-style verifiable items plus a held-out set of grade-school math and factual QA with gold answers) and to MT-bench and LLMBar prompts; every cross-family pair is judged by every judge in both orders. Model: mixed-effects logistic regression of P(judge prefers A) on objective quality difference, same_family(judge, A), position, length difference, with random intercepts for prompt; the pre-registered test is the same_family coefficient, with swap-corrected neutral rates and third-judge adjudication as references for open-ended items. Stage 3 (exploratory): judge perplexity on each candidate as mediator (Wataoka mechanism); size scaling within Qwen (0.5B-4B); self/other label manipulation following 'Self- and Other-Labels Induce Bidirectional Bias in LLM Judges' (EMNLP Findings 2026 per its arXiv comment); two prompt templates; rubric and reasoning-on/off sensitivity; contamination probes (testset-slot guessing) on benchmark items. Hypotheses: H1 kappa deflation >= 30 points for every judge on MT-bench; H2 swap consistency < 0.8 for every <= 4B judge; H3 at least one 3-4B judge reaches kappa >= 0.4 on LLMBar-Natural and none reaches kappa >= 0.2 on LLMBar-Adversarial or JudgeBench; H4 same_family coefficient > 0 after quality control; H5 4-bit versus 8-bit changes kappa by less than 0.05. Unit of analysis: judgment nested in item, judge, quantisation, order and run. Compute: the full design (about 10,000 pairs x 2 orders x 3 runs x 14 judge-quantisation cells) is cut to a preregistered subsample (about 1,500 pairs for 3-4B judges; 1.5-2B judges on everything), roughly 20-40k judgments at 5-30 s each on 4 cores, run in background over several days.

Perplexities computed with the same judge weights.
ideas.risks: Validity: benchmark items may be in the 2025 models' training data (contamination probes mitigate, not remove); small human-labelled sets give wide intervals (Bowyer et al.), so claims are about intervals, not point ranks; MT-bench votes come mostly from student labellers, so kappa against them is an upper bound on human validity; stated-confidence calibration may be unavailable for some models; small judges may sit near chance on hard pairs, leaving the leakage test underpowered (then the result is the validity floor and the factorial is restricted to items where judges exceed chance); objective-label tasks exclude stylistic preference, so leakage on open-ended quality is out of scope; family membership is coarse (Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 share lineage), so a pre-specified family taxonomy is needed; quantisation level and chat-template differences across families are confounds (same quant level, two templates, both reported); third-judge adjudication for open-ended items is a single-rater reference and must be reported as such. Execution: prefill of two-response prompts on CPU costs tens of seconds per judgment for 3-4B models, so subsampling is fixed in advance; the cohort study's pending data release could pre-empt part of the validity table; model-version drift is avoided by pinning Hugging Face revisions; JudgeBench and the leakage code live partly on GitHub.
ideas.journal_audience: ACL, EMNLP or NAACL main or Findings; the GEM workshop on evaluation; Transactions on Machine Learning Research. IS secondary audience: Business & Information Systems Engineering (methods for AI-based IS) or an evaluation-methods note in Information Systems Frontiers.
ideas.undermining_evidence: A paper reporting kappa, swap consistency and calibration-set intervals for <= 4B open judges on LLMBar, JudgeBench or MT-bench would remove RQ1-RQ2; the arXiv search found only Tiwari (7-8B, correlation only) and Zhao, Wang and Chen (12-14B, different question), but Semantic Scholar answered HTTP 429 to the targeted query and the cohort study's dataset release is pending, so a repeat search is required. If the full text of Thakur et al. (GEM 2025; arXiv 2406.12624) already reports chance-corrected validity for 1-4B judges on the same datasets and crosses judge and exam-taker families, Stage 1 is a replication and Stage 2 loses novelty; if Norman et al.'s 21 judges include several sub-4B open models with kappa (model sizes not shown in the abstract), the validity table is partly done; if the Preference Leakage appendix or the 2026 'Self- and Other-Labels' paper already shows a null same-family effect for small open judges without fine-tuning, RQ3 is answered; if Lee et al.'s correction already ships with small-judge experiments (abstract only read), the calibration-curve contribution shrinks. If every small judge is at chance on every subset, H3 fails and the leakage test is uninterpretable; the paper then stands as a negative result plus the calibration curves.

ideas.working_title: Gaming the AI Rater: Self-Presentation Cues and Embedded Instructions in LLM-Based Evaluation of Employee Work Products
ideas.problem_rq: When an organization lets an LLM rate worker outputs (code changes, customer-service replies, written reports), the rated worker controls the text being judged. RQ1: How much do low-effort, non-technical cues that a worker could add (assertive self-assessment, seniority or tenure claims, prior-rating anchors, a 'note to reviewer' instruction, politeness or effort signals) shift ratings from small, locally deployable open models, relative to the ratings' sensitivity to actual quality? RQ2: How often do such cues produce rank reversals in which a gamed low-quality item outranks an un-gamed high-quality item? RQ3: Which cheap mitigations (stripping author metadata, rubric-anchored scoring, reference-guided grading, pairwise scoring with order swap) reduce gameability for 1-4B judges, and at what cost in quality sensitivity?
ideas.why_matters: Rating is one of Kellogg et al.'s six algorithmic-control mechanisms; Dong et al. show ratings from an AI manager are accepted with muted emotional response; Sum et al. document workers' obfuscation and gaming tactics under surveillance. Under the EU AI Act, AI that evaluates workers is high-risk and must meet accuracy and robustness obligations. If a sentence of self-praise or an embedded instruction moves a rating as much as a real quality difference, LLM-based evaluation rewards gaming rather than performance (a Goodhart dynamic) and penalizes workers who do not game, a fairness and validity problem for any LLM-enabled monitoring system. The evaluation digest's gaps G5 and G6 state that no record received tests submitter-side sycophancy or enterprise-document injection with small open backbones. Stakeholders: rated workers, HR and line managers, vendors of monitoring and performance tools, works councils and regulators.
ideas.contribution: Empirical plus design contribution with an IS framing. (1) Empirical: effect sizes of worker-controllable cues on LLM ratings, expressed as a gaming-to-signal ratio against the ratings' quality sensitivity, with rank-reversal rates and chance-corrected agreement with ground truth. (2) Design knowledge: which scoring formats and sanitization steps make small on-premise judges robust, the deployment regime a cost-constrained employer would use. (3) Theory: extends measurement-gaming and control theory to LLM-mediated rating, where the cost of gaming falls from effortful behaviour to a sentence of text. A null would establish a robustness floor for small judges and still deliver the audit protocol. The judge models, datasets and llama.cpp harness are shared with the small-judge validation idea, so the two can run as one program.

ideas.difference: Raina, Liusie and Gales (EMNLP 2024) and Shi et al. (CCS 2024) attack judges with optimized universal suffixes or gradient-based injections, technical attacks a typical worker would not craft; 'Cheating Automatic LLM Benchmarks' (arXiv 2410.07137, ICLR 2025 Oral per the arXiv comment) uses constant null responses against benchmarks. Dong et al. study worker reactions to AI ratings, not manipulation of them. Zheng et al. measure position and verbosity bias, not submitter self-presentation. ideas.design: Within-artefact factorial experiment, no human participants. ideas.working_title: Published but Uninformative? Sampling Uncertainty, Exclusion Rules and the Evidentiary Value of NYC Local Law 144 Impact Ratios
ideas.problem_rq: Local Law 144 requires employers to publish impact ratios from a bias audit but sets no threshold, lets auditors choose a selection-rate (binary pass) or scoring-rate (above-median) definition, allows categories under 2% of the sample and 'unknown' demographic categories to be excluded, and lets vendors pool data across many employers. Wright et al. (FAccT 2024, read in full) found 96% of 386 published ratios at or above 0.8 and 20% omitted under the 2% rule; Gerchick et al. (FAccT 2025, abstract) found missing demographic data, opaque aggregation and metrics that do not reflect use; Lam et al. (FAccT 2024) list a UGESP statistical-significance criterion that LL 144 itself does not require. None of these quantifies how much evidence a published ratio carries. The OSF archive of Wright et al. (osf.io/upfdk, public, downloaded on 2026-10-03) holds 449 impact-ratio rows and 80 audit PDFs, several of which report per-category applicant and selected counts (the Bloomberg report lists 250 Black female applicants, 189 selected, ratio 0.83; the BNP Paribas report lists tens of thousands per category and 200,486 applicants excluded as unknown). RQ1: Given the counts actually published, what share of LL 144 impact ratios are statistically distinguishable from the 0.8 convention, and how large are the excluded 'unknown' and sub-2% populations relative to the audited ones? RQ2: In calibrated simulations, how do the rules' discretionary choices (2% exclusion, unknown exclusion, scoring- versus selection-rate, intersectional splitting, pooling across employers or jobs) change the probability that a tool with a true impact ratio below 0.8 publishes a ratio at or above 0.8, and vice versa? RQ3: Which reporting designs (interval estimates, posterior probability of disparity, UGESP two-standard-deviation test, minimum detectable disparity statements) would make published ratios informative at the sample sizes observed?
ideas.why_matters: Transparency-based accountability regimes depend on published numbers being interpretable; if most published ratios are compatible with both compliance and substantial disparity at the published sample sizes, or if the exclusion rules remove exactly the small groups most likely to be harmed, then the 'null compliance' problem extends from whether audits are published to whether published audits can inform anyone. The result bears on the governance digest's gap that no outcome evidence exists for audit mandates and on the design of EU AI Act conformity reporting. The simulation toolkit and the reanalysed corpus are reusable by regulators and auditors.
ideas.contribution: Measurement methodology and empirical reanalysis (FAccT-style). (1) A reanalysis of a public corpus of real bias-audit reports that attaches interval estimates and posterior disparity probabilities to published point ratios and quantifies excluded populations. (2) A simulation framework, calibrated to the empirical distribution of category sizes and selection rates, that estimates false-pass and false-fail rates of the LL 144 reporting rule as a function of sample size, category share, metric choice, intersectional splitting and pooling. (3) A comparison of alternative reporting designs with a concrete 'minimum informative sample' statement. If the published counts turn out large enough that ratios are precise, the contribution shifts to the exclusion and aggregation effects, which remains a policy-relevant finding.

ideas.working_title: Productivity Scores from Workflow Traces: How Robust Are Log-Derived Worker Performance Rankings to Defensible Measurement Choices?
ideas.problem_rq: Employee monitoring and people-analytics systems increasingly compute worker performance scores from workflow and transaction logs (events with timestamps and resource identifiers), yet the algorithmic-management records received measure monitoring only through self-report scales and none audits what such scores actually measure. RQ1: Across a space of defensible scoring configurations (metric definition, attribution rule, time window, idle-time threshold, case-mix adjustment), how stable are the resulting worker rankings and bottom/top-quintile memberships in real organizational event logs? RQ2: Which configuration dimension contributes most to ranking variance, and does case-mix adjustment systematically reorder workers who handle harder cases? RQ3: Can an auditable robustness protocol (rank-stability, reclassification and impact-ratio analogues) be specified so that deployers, works councils and data-protection officers can test a monitoring metric before it is used for decisions about people?
ideas.why_matters: Ravid et al.'s meta-analysis finds monitoring does not raise performance but does raise stress and privacy invasion; Kellogg et al. identify 'rating' as a core algorithmic-control mechanism; Oezdemir et al. show supervisors absorb accountability for scores they cannot interpret. Under the EU AI Act, AI used to evaluate or monitor workers is listed as high-risk and deployers must enable human oversight, yet no record received pairs system-logged activity with the scores built from it (human-AI digest gap 3: exposure measured by perception, not telemetry). If plausible configurations produce different 'worst performers', then score-based decisions are measurement artefacts and oversight needs a robustness test, not just a human in the loop. Stakeholders: monitored workers, line supervisors, HR and works councils, DPOs and labour regulators, and vendors of monitoring dashboards.
ideas.contribution: IS contribution with an organizational problem (worker evaluation from workflow traces) and identified stakeholders. (1) Empirical: direct quantification, on public real-life event logs, of how much worker rankings move across defensible scoring configurations, with variance decomposition over configuration factors. (2) Design-science artefact: an open, pm4py-based 'monitoring-metric robustness audit' protocol (rank-stability coefficients with bootstrap CIs, quintile-reclassification rates, case-mix confounding tests, four-fifths-style ratios across resource roles) evaluated on several logs. (3) Theoretical mechanism: links measurement-validity concepts (reliability, construct confounding by case mix, Simpson-type reversals) to the rating mechanism of algorithmic control, explaining why transparency about a metric is not the same as validity of a metric. If rankings converge, that is itself a usable reassurance result and the artefact remains.

ideas.working_title: Would the Claim Survive an Error Bar? Auditing Statistical and Judge-Validation Practice in Published LLM Evaluations in IS and Industry-Track Venues
ideas.problem_rq: Published LLM evaluations are used as evidence by IS researchers and practitioners, yet three bodies of methods work (Miller 2024 on clustered standard errors; Bowyer et al. 2025 on CLT failure below a few hundred items; Atil et al. on up-to-15% run-to-run accuracy variation) imply that many single-run point differences are within noise, and Norman et al. (2026 preprint) show raw judge agreement overstates chance-corrected agreement by 33-41 points. No audit of IS venues appeared in the records received (domain-filtered queries returned no IS hits and an arXiv API query for IS reporting audits returned nothing relevant). RQ1: Among empirical LLM-evaluation papers published 2023-2026 in IS journals with fetchable full text (BISE, Information Systems Frontiers, Electronic Markets; ICIS/ECIS where PDFs can be obtained) and in ACL/EMNLP/NAACL industry tracks, what share report item counts, repeated runs, decoding settings, model identifier with version or date, any uncertainty (SE/CI), and, when an LLM judge is used, human validation with a chance-corrected agreement statistic? RQ2: For each paper's headline comparison claim for which n and accuracies are reported, what share of reported differences exceed the interval implied by the paper's own n under (a) a naive binomial SE, (b) Miller-style clustered SE with an ICC sensitivity range, and (c) a Bayesian Beta-Binomial interval in the Bowyer et al. regime, i.e. what is the 'claim survival rate'? RQ3: Does survival differ between IS and industry-NLP venues and over time?
ideas.why_matters: IS is accumulating LLM evaluation results fast (Crossref on 2026-10-03: 16 BISE, 24 ISF, 15 Electronic Markets, 27 I&M and 41 DSS articles since 2023 with 'language model' in the title) and the ISJ editorial on artifact under-specification exists because reporting is thin. The ICSE 2026 replication found none of five executable LLM studies fully reproducible; Bean et al. (NeurIPS 2025) found construct-validity problems across 445 CS benchmarks. If a large share of IS headline claims are statistically indistinguishable from noise under their own reported n, then organizational decisions and follow-on theorizing built on them rest on unstable quantities (the GenAI digest already lists version and reporting inconsistencies across arXiv, NBER and journal versions of the same studies). The audit yields an evidence-based reporting checklist for IS editors and reviewers, useful whatever the survival rate turns out to be.
ideas.contribution: IS meta-research contribution (organizational problem: decision-makers and researchers relying on evaluation claims; stakeholders: IS editors, reviewers, authors, and practitioners selecting LLM systems). Empirical: coded prevalence of reporting elements with Wilson CIs, cross-field comparison with the ICSE 2026 and Bean et al. figures as CS comparators, and the claim-survival re-analysis. Methodological: a small standard-library Python tool that takes reported n, accuracies and optional cluster structure and returns survival under the three uncertainty models, released with the coding protocol so the audit can be repeated on new volumes. Theoretical: a decomposition of evaluation-claim fragility into sampling (n), procedure (runs, decoding), identity (model version) and measurement (judge validity) components.

ideas.working_title: Documentation as Audit Evidence: How Often Do Self-Reported Model-Card Benchmark Scores Agree with Independent Evaluations of the Same Checkpoint?
ideas.problem_rq: Algorithm-audit frameworks rely on auditee documentation (Lam et al.'s indirect verification; Raji et al.'s design history file), the EU AI Act's technical-documentation duties assume self-reported evaluation results are informative, and Liang et al. found evaluation sections among the least complete in 32,111 Hugging Face model cards, yet no record received measures whether the evaluation numbers that are documented are accurate. The Open LLM Leaderboard independently re-evaluated thousands of Hugging Face checkpoints with a fixed harness and recorded the checkpoint sha and per-task standard errors (open-llm-leaderboard-old/results: 10,160 result files; open-llm-leaderboard/results: 10,510; both ungated), while many of those models' cards carry author-typed benchmark tables (e.g. zephyr-7b-beta's README reports MT-Bench 7.34 and AlpacaEval 90.60 in a markdown table) that are distinguishable from bot-populated model-index entries whose source field names the leaderboard. RQ1: Among independently evaluated models, what share of cards state any benchmark result, and what share state it verifiably (benchmark, metric, n-shot, harness or version, checkpoint)? RQ2: Among verifiable self-reported scores on a benchmark the leaderboard also ran for the same checkpoint sha, how large and how directional is the discrepancy, expressed in units of the independent standard error, and how does it compare with the leaderboard's own re-evaluation noise floor (models with two result files)? RQ3: What predicts discrepancy and verifiability (organization type, downloads, license, base vs fine-tune or merge, release date, presence of a bot-populated model-index)?
ideas.why_matters: Deployers choose open models from documentation, auditors verify documentation rather than re-run evaluations, and regulators are about to accept technical documentation as conformity evidence (governance digest gaps 3 and 5). Wright et al. and Gerchick et al. show that under LL 144 published audit numbers are incomplete and probably publication-biased, and Lin et al. argue compliance data is not evaluation data; a measured base rate of misstatement in the most widely used public documentation corpus tells auditors whether documentation can be sampled and trusted, and tells IS researchers whether 'documented performance' is a valid construct. The Leaderboard Illusion documents gaming of human-preference leaderboards; this study documents the complementary question of whether self-reports agree with independent measurement.
ideas.contribution: Empirical: a platform-scale estimate of self-report versus independent-evaluation agreement for the same checkpoint, with a noise floor from repeated independent runs, and a verifiability profile of evaluation claims in model cards. Methodological: a coding scheme for the verifiability of an evaluation claim (benchmark, metric, configuration, checkpoint identity, source) usable in audit protocols and in the EU AI Act technical-documentation context. IS/governance contribution: documentation as an organizational control whose reliability can be quantified; stakeholders are deployers selecting models, internal and external auditors, platform operators and regulators. A null result (self-reports agree within noise) is as useful as a positive one because it licenses sampled documentation verification.

ideas.difference: Liang et al. and Bhat et al. measure whether sections are filled and what topics they cover, not whether the numbers are right; this study checks numbers against an independent re-run of the identical checkpoint. Lam et al. define indirect verification of auditee documentation but give no base rate for misstatement; this supplies one. The Leaderboard Illusion studies selective disclosure on a human-preference arena; here the comparison is self-report versus harness re-evaluation on static benchmarks with recorded standard errors and shas. Lin et al. argue conceptually that compliance data is not evaluation data; this is an empirical test on documentation that functions as compliance evidence. Two 2026 preprints seen only via the arXiv API ('Evaluation Cards: An Interpretive Layer for AI Evaluation Reporting', which proposes a reporting layer, and 'AI Transparency Atlas', which scores documentation of five frontier models) do not measure discrepancy at scale.
ideas.design: Unit of analysis: model-benchmark claim, clustered by model and by uploading organization. Population: all models listed in open-llm-leaderboard-old/requests and open-llm-leaderboard/requests with a results file (about 16k request files; v1 covers ARC 25-shot, HellaSwag 10-shot, MMLU 5-shot, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, GSM8K with acc and acc_stderr; v2 covers IFEval, BBH, MATH, GPQA, MUSR, MMLU-PRO with stderrs and model_sha). Card acquisition: README and cardData for each model via the Hub API (observed limit 500 requests per 300 s, about 3 hours), plus the 2023 davanstrien/model_cards_with_readmes snapshot for historical card versions and the Zenodo August 2026 metadata CSV for covariates (downloads, licenses, arXiv ids, base_model). Claim extraction without any LLM: model-index entries classified by source (leaderboard bot versus other); markdown tables and inline statements parsed by regex for the twelve benchmark names, metric names and numbers; a 300-card stratified sample hand-coded by two coders to estimate extraction precision and recall with kappa, thresholds fixed before analysis. Verifiability score per claim (benchmark named; metric named; n-shot or config; harness or version; checkpoint or revision; source). Discrepancy = self-reported minus independent score for the same sha and benchmark, divided by the independent stderr; noise floor = the same statistic between two independent result files of the same model. Confirmatory, pre-registered: H1 the mean signed discrepancy is positive (self-reports exceed independent scores); H2 discrepancies for claims lacking configuration are larger in absolute value than for configured claims; H3 cards with a bot-populated model-index contain fewer author-reported claims. Exploratory: regressions of |discrepancy| and verifiability on organization type (company, academic, individual), downloads, license, fine-tune/merge status, release date; relation to the leaderboard's Flagged field; time trend from v1 to v2. Baselines: the noise floor; a permutation null pairing self-reports with other models' independent scores. Analysis in numpy/scipy/statsmodels on CPU.
ideas.data_resources: Hugging Face datasets, ungated per the Hub API on 2026-10-03: open-llm-leaderboard-old/results (10,160 files), open-llm-leaderboard-old/requests (10,047), open-llm-leaderboard-old/contents (one parquet), open-llm-leaderboard/results (10,510 files), open-llm-leaderboard/requests (5,987), open-llm-leaderboard/contents (one parquet; license field None, so terms must be checked before redistribution); Hugging Face Hub API model endpoints and raw README files (per-repository licenses); davanstrien/model_cards_with_readmes (license field empty); Zenodo record 22918529 'Hugging Face Model Cards Metadata Dataset' (CC-BY-4.0; 465 MB CSV, August 2026); a model's result JSON downloaded in this session contains config_general with model_sha and per-task acc_stderr. No LLM or embedding model required.
ideas.risks: Validity: legitimate configuration differences (few-shot count, harness version, chat template) can produce discrepancies that are not misstatements, so claims are stratified by configuration completeness and the headline is the verifiability profile, with discrepancy reported only for configuration-matched claims; regex extraction will miss or mis-parse some tables (precision and recall estimated on the hand-coded sample and propagated as bounds); the leaderboard population over-represents hobbyist fine-tunes and merges, so results describe the public ecosystem deployers draw from, not frontier vendors, and organization type is a stratifier; the leaderboard was archived in March 2025, so the study is retrospective; multiple benchmarks per model require clustered inference. Execution: about 16k API calls under the 500-per-300-s limit; result files total several gigabytes (fits in 30 GB disk); licensing of the leaderboard datasets is not shown and must be confirmed before releasing derived tables; author-reported numbers may be rare for small uploaders, which would shrink RQ2's sample while leaving RQ1 and RQ3 intact.
ideas.journal_audience: ACM FAccT or AIES (audit and documentation practice); Nature Machine Intelligence or Patterns as a follow-up to Liang et al.; IS: Information Systems Frontiers, Journal of the AIS or Business & Information Systems Engineering (AI governance and documentation as control).
ideas.undermining_evidence: A published large-scale comparison of self-reported model-card scores with independent re-evaluation of the same checkpoints (arXiv API queries on 'model cards' with 'leaderboard' and 'self-reported', and a Semantic Scholar query on verifiability of model-card claims, returned only reporting frameworks, a five-model documentation analysis and an automated card-generation pipeline; three further Semantic Scholar queries answered HTTP 429 and the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so a targeted search of the Hugging Face papers index and FAccT 2025-2026 proceedings is the first check). The idea also collapses if extraction finds that almost no leaderboard-evaluated cards carry author-reported benchmark numbers other than the bot-populated entries, which would leave only the verifiability descriptive.

ideas.working_title: Does Quantization Hurt Bangla More? A CPU-Only Factorial of Precision, Model Size and Script for Generative and Retrieval Models, with a Cost-Matched Lexical-versus-Dense Frontier for Bengali, Swahili and Indonesian
ideas.problem_rq: Whether post-training quantization is language-neutral is unresolved: Borgersen and Goodwin find no significant effect of GGUF k-quantization (Llama 3.3 70B, English and Norwegian), Marchisio et al. and Marie and Fujita find larger harm for non-Latin-script and low-resource languages and for smaller models (GPTQ/bitsandbytes/AWQ and multiple formats, 1.7B-103B), and the newest Bangla-specific study (Hossain, Shafin and Al Mumin 2026, arXiv 2608.24615) tests only 7B-20B models at 8-bit on multiple-choice NLU and concludes that architecture and format matter more than bit width. On the retrieval side, the 'simple wins' results (BM25 leading above about 10 million corpus tokens in Wang et al.; dense+BM25 hybrid best in HERB; LLM bi-encoders adding latency for modest gains in Abdallah et al.) are English-only and measured without a CPU budget, and the only cost-free comparison received for the target languages is the MIRACL dev baseline table (bn: BM25 0.508, mDPR 0.443, hybrid 0.654 nDCG@10; id: 0.449, 0.272, 0.443; sw: 0.383, 0.299, 0.446), which shows the lexical-dense balance differs by language but reports no latency, memory or index cost and uses a 2022 zero-shot mDPR. No record received crosses quantizer level down to 2-4 bits, model size in the CPU-deployable 1-4B range, script and organizational task type on the same items, nor tests whether encoder quantization harm is script-dependent. RQ1 (generative): For 1-4B instruction-tuned models run through llama.cpp on a 4-core CPU, how does relative quality loss at Q8_0, Q6_K, Q4_K_M, Q3_K_M and Q2_K (versus bf16) vary with script and language (Bangla versus Latin-script Swahili and Indonesian, English as control), model size and task type (classification, reading comprehension, extractive QA, summarization), once tokenizer fertility is included in the cost? RQ2 (retrieval): Under matched CPU budgets, when does a small multilingual embedder (fp32 or int8) or a BM25+dense hybrid beat tokenization-aware BM25 for bn, sw and id, does the answer change with corpus-size tier, and is the quality loss from int8 encoder quantization larger for Bangla than for Latin-script languages? RQ3 (joint): Does the script x precision interaction have the same sign and comparable magnitude in decoders and encoders, i.e. is script-dependent quantization harm a property of the language rather than of the model class?
ideas.why_matters: A quantized 1-4B model plus a CPU retrieval stack is the only private, CPU-only option an SME or local public office in a low-resource-language country has (efficiency digest gaps 1, 2 and 4); if 4-bit quantization or int8 encoders silently cost Bangla users several points more than English users, deployment guides written from English benchmarks mislead exactly the organizations with the least slack. Conversely, a null interaction at small sizes under GGUF would reconcile the published contradiction (format rather than language as the driver) and license cheaper deployments. The fertility-adjusted cost term matters because Mahfuz et al. report inefficient Bengali tokenization, so cost per document, not per token, is the relevant quantity. The retrieval frontier answers a concrete deployment question (is an embedding model worth its CPU at all?) for three languages with 400 million-plus speakers and tests whether the English scaling result of Wang et al. transfers.
ideas.contribution: Empirical contribution to the efficiency-by-language literature: (1) a pre-registered factorial replication that holds tasks and items constant across languages (Belebele and Global-MMLU are parallel across bn, sw, id and en), measures degradation at bit widths the Bangla study did not reach, includes the smallest deployable sizes, and reports a costed CPU frontier with fertility-adjusted cost per item; (2) a cost-matched retrieval frontier (nDCG@10 and Recall@100 per CPU-second, per gigabyte of RAM and per index byte) with tokenization-aware BM25 variants, int8 encoders and hybrids across corpus tiers, replicating the corpus-scale crossover in non-English settings; (3) a joint test of whether quantization harm is script-dependent across two model classes, extending the quantization-by-language literature from generation to retrieval; (4) released configurations and a public results table that SMEs can use as a model- and retrieval-stack selection aid. If the interaction hypotheses fail, the frontier, the fertility-adjusted cost analysis and the reconciliation of the Borgersen-versus-Marchisio contradiction at small sizes remain publishable.

ideas.difference: Marchisio et al. use 8B-103B models, GPU quantizers and languages the models already support, and state that deterioration is likely larger for truly low-resource languages; Borgersen and Goodwin test one 70B model under GGUF on two Latin-script languages; Marie and Fujita cover 55 languages and GGUF but only machine translation with automatic metrics; Hossain et al. cover Bangla NLU at 8-bit for 7B-20B models; Chimoto et al. study calibration-language effects for GPTQ/AWQ at 7-8B on perplexity. MIRACL and Mr. TyDi report BM25 versus zero-shot mDPR versus a fixed hybrid on GPUs with no cost accounting and no tokenization variants; Wang et al. vary corpus scale and cost only in English with an LLM reader and judge; Abdallah et al. measure efficiency of LLM-based retrievers on BRIGHT (English reasoning), not small encoders in low-resource languages; Reza et al. evaluate one Bengali domain collection with six embedders without cost, corpus scale or quantization. This design is the missing factorial cell on both sides: GGUF k-quant levels down to Q2_K and int8 ONNX encoders, 1-4B decoders and 118-278M encoders, Bangla versus Swahili versus Indonesian versus English on parallel items, organizational task types and human-judged retrieval sets only (no LLM judge), measured CPU throughput and RAM, and tokenizer fertility folded into cost.
ideas.design: Part A, generative factorial. Models (all reachable without login): Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B (apache-2.0, official GGUF repos), Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (apache-2.0) and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (license 'other'), gemma-3-4b-it via unsloth GGUF (gemma license), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct via unsloth GGUF (llama3.2 license), TigerLLM-1B-it (cc-by-4.0, converted to GGUF locally), sarvam-1 (license tag not shown). Precision: bf16 reference on CPU, Q8_0, Q6_K, Q4_K_M, Q3_K_M, Q2_K. Languages: bn, sw, id, en. Tasks and measures: Belebele reading comprehension (accuracy; identical passages across languages), Global-MMLU (accuracy), IndoNLU SmSA, MasakhaNEWS Swahili and a Bangla sentiment set (macro-F1), squad_bn extractive QA (F1), XL-Sum summarization on 200 items per language (chrF, ROUGE-L), Bangladesh legal QA as an organizational-domain extension. Cost: tokens per second, CPU-seconds per item, peak RAM, tokens per character per tokenizer. Three seeded greedy runs per cell; bf16 reference restricted to 500 items per task where CPU time forces it. Part B, retrieval frontier. Unit: query x configuration x language (MIRACL dev: bn 411 queries, id 960, sw 482; Mr. TyDi dev/test for replication). Factors: retriever family (whitespace BM25 floor; tokenization-aware BM25 with language analyzers, character n-grams, SentencePiece subwords, RM3 feedback; multilingual-e5-small 118M, multilingual-e5-base 278M, paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 118M in fp32 and ONNX int8; bge-m3 as upper bound on smaller tiers; hybrids via RRF and linear fusion with alpha tuned on a held-out split), language (bn, sw, id, en control), corpus tier (five nested random subsets of each MIRACL corpus up to full, judged passages kept fixed as in Wang et al.; sw 131,924 passages, bn 297,265, id 1,446,315). Measures: nDCG@10, Recall@100, indexing CPU-seconds, index bytes, p50/p95 query latency on 4 cores (three repeated runs), peak RAM. Confirmatory, pre-registered: H1 language x precision interaction in decoders (relative loss at Q4_K_M and below larger for bn than for sw/id/en), mixed-effects logistic regression on item-level correctness with random intercepts for parallel items and models; H2 size x precision interaction (smaller models lose more); H3 fertility-adjusted cost per Bangla item exceeds English by a factor of at least two at equal precision; H4 tokenization-aware BM25 improves nDCG@10 over whitespace BM25 more for bn than for id; H5 the relative nDCG@10 loss from int8 encoder quantization is larger for bn than for sw, id and en (language x precision in a mixed-effects model over queries); H6 the hybrid's margin over BM25 shrinks with corpus tier. Joint analysis (RQ3): standardized interaction estimates from H1 and H5 compared with their intervals. Exploratory: task-type moderation, refusal and language-drift rates (Mahadi et al. 2026 observed small models drifting from Bangla into English), reconciliation analysis comparing GGUF at 8-bit with Hossain et al.'s reported pattern, Pareto frontiers per language and model class, query-type analysis (colloquial versus formal) using the AgriTrust-RAG collection if it becomes resolvable. Statistics: paired bootstrap over items or queries with Holm correction. Scope control: a preregistered reduction plan (bge-m3 restricted to the two smallest tiers; bf16 capped at 500 items per task; generation tasks capped at 200 items); if the joint paper is too long, Part B is reported as a companion reproducibility-track paper citing the shared hypotheses.
ideas.data_resources: Generative tasks on Hugging Face, not gated: facebook/belebele (cc-by-sa-4.0, bn/sw/id/en), CohereLabs/Global-MMLU (apache-2.0), indonlp/indonlu (MIT), masakhane/masakhanews (afl-3.0), csebuetnlp/xlsum (cc-by-nc-sa-4.0, research use), csebuetnlp/squad_bn (cc-by-nc-sa-4.0), Bangla sentiment candidates ragibhasan/coke_studio_bangla_sentiment (apache-2.0) and TanjimKIT/Bangla_Sentiments_in_eLearning (apache-2.0, provenance to be audited), tabularisai/swahili-sentiment-dataset (apache-2.0), momahadi/bangladesh-legal-qa-dataset (cc-by-4.0). Retrieval: miracl/miracl and miracl/miracl-corpus (apache-2.0, not gated), castorini/mr-tydi and castorini/mr-tydi-corpus (apache-2.0); optional RaiyanKhaan/AgriTrust-RAG (URL in the arXiv 2608.14886 abstract; the HF API returned no record for it on 2026-10-03). Encoders: intfloat/multilingual-e5-small and -base (MIT), sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 (apache-2.0), BAAI/bge-m3 (MIT). Decoders as listed in the design, all reachable through the Hugging Face API without login; the gated originals (google/gemma-3-4b-it, meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, both gated 'manual'; CohereLabs/tiny-aya-base gated 'auto' and non-commercial) are avoided via ungated GGUF mirrors; FLORES+ (gated) is not required. Tooling from PyPI: llama-cpp-python, lm-evaluation-harness, bm25s or rank_bm25 (pyserini requires Java, which may be absent), sentencepiece, onnxruntime, sentence-transformers.
ideas.risks: Validity: automatic metrics understate quantization harm by an order of magnitude relative to human judgment in Marchisio et al., so summarization conclusions are weak without native-speaker rating (no participants available; confirmatory claims are restricted to exact-match tasks and human-judged retrieval sets); Belebele and Global-MMLU are translated, not native organizational text, and MIRACL passages are Wikipedia, not invoices or circulars; the Bangla sentiment sets on the Hub have unclear provenance; ungated GGUF mirrors may differ from original weights, so a local conversion from the ungated Qwen checkpoints anchors the comparison; dense encoders may have seen MIRACL during training; nested-tier subsampling changes the distractor distribution; pure-Python BM25 tokenizers differ from the Anserini analyzers used in published baselines. Execution: bf16 inference of a 4B model on 4 cores is a few tokens per second and bge-m3 encoding of 1.4 million Indonesian passages takes days, so the full factorial is weeks of CPU time and the preregistered reduction plan is mandatory; 15 GB RAM excludes bf16 above about 5B; latency measurements on a shared container are noisy; licence terms (gemma, llama3.2) restrict redistribution of derived artefacts but not evaluation; the merged scope is large and may need to be split into two companion papers.
ideas.journal_audience: Findings of ACL/EMNLP or the EMNLP Industry Track (efficiency and multilinguality) for the quantization factorial; ECIR reproducibility track or SIGIR resource track, Information Processing & Management or ACM TOIS for the retrieval frontier; LREC-COLING for the resource and evaluation angle; Information Systems Frontiers or the Electronic Journal of Information Systems in Developing Countries for an IS-framed version on deployment choices of resource-constrained organizations.
ideas.undermining_evidence: An extension of Hossain et al. (or a paper inside Miranda et al.'s 232-paper survey, read at abstract level only) that already reports 1-4B GGUF results at 4-bit and below across scripts on comparable tasks; the per-language appendix of Marie and Fujita showing no script interaction for small models under GGUF, which would pre-empt H1 for the MT task; the ICADEIS 2026 paper 'Evaluating Sparse-Dense Hybrid Fusion Strategies on the Indonesian Mr. TyDi Benchmark' (Saragih et al., abstract not shown), which should be read first and, if it covers cost and quantization for Indonesian, removes that language from Part B; evidence that int8 encoder quantization has negligible effect for all scripts (kills H5 but leaves the frontier); an outcome in which bf16 small models are already at chance on Bangla tasks (BenLLM-Eval found open LLaMA-2 'significantly bad'), which would leave no headroom to measure degradation and force a switch to fine-tuned task models; or modern small encoders beating tokenization-tuned BM25 by a wide margin at every tier and budget, which would turn Part B into a negative result for lexical retrieval.
